multiplechoiceresponse.p: What makes a pilot result trustworthy?

choice.div: A baseline, measures that include review and rework, and a stopping rule agreed in advance.
Participants saying they liked the tool.
A large time saving measured only on the assisted step.

div.p: Net gain includes the cost of review and rework, and the stopping rule keeps the report honest.

multiplechoiceresponse.p: A workflow saves ten minutes per case and adds fifteen minutes of review. What is the conclusion?

choice.div: It is a net loss in time; redesign the check or stop.
It is a success because the assisted step is faster.

div.p: The unit of improvement is the whole process, not the assisted step.

choice.div: Runbook, named owner, training, and a tested rollback.
A slide deck for the sponsor.

div.p: An owner and a rollback are what make the workflow operable by someone else.

multiplechoiceresponse.p: Which failure mode is most likely to reach a customer unnoticed?

choice.div: A confident, wrong policy statement in an otherwise well-written reply.
A blank field that stops the workflow.
A syntax error in the output format.

div.p: Visible failures are caught by controls. Plausible wrong content is what needs a source check.

choiceresponse.p: Which practices keep an assisted workflow safe over time? Select all that apply.

choice.div: Naming the person who owns the output.
Testing the failure modes before the pilot.
Removing the review step once error rates look low.

div.p: Ownership, testing, fallback and re-measurement keep the workflow honest. A low error rate is not a reason to remove the control that produced it.
